newsitem.title: UK: FEATURE - Obsession with sex dates back four million years.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Obsession with sex dates back four million years.

text.p: Our prehistoric ancestors were just as obsessed by sex as we are, according to an archaeologist who has taken a sweeping look at four million years of passion.
Timothy Taylor argues that masturbation, homosexuality, bestiality and transvestism date back to the early mists of time. Sex has never been just for reproduction, he says.
Graphic proof is offered by a 5,000-year-old Siberian rock engraving of a Stone Age man on skis trying to penetrate an elk.
Black Sea Scythian nomads, made impotent by the constant jolting they received on horseback, wore women's clothing.
Amazonian women cauterised one breast of their baby daughters so they could shoot their bows more effectively when they grew up. Only women who had killed three people were allowed to breed.

"Our species have been around for over 100,000 years with the same underlying curiosities and fascinations about life and death," says Taylor, a lecturer in archaeology at the University of Bradford in northern England.

"As soon as there are written records, from around 5,000 years ago in the Far East, we find references to many of the sexual practices -- homosexuality, male and female transsexualism and transvestism, masturbation -- familiar to us today."
SEXUAL IMAGERY DATES BACK 30,000 YEARS
Examples abound in Taylor's entertaining "The Prehistory of Sex" to underline his point that sexual imagery dates back at least 30,000 years. Eroticism, not biology ruled way back then.
The chapter headings certainly inspire the reader to keep turning the pages -- "Making the Beast with Two Backs," "The Graves of the Golden Penis" and "Skull Sex and Brain Sex."
Taylor peers into graves, gawps at cave paintings and quotes everyone from Hippocrates to feminist Germaine Greer to bring a popular touch to his academic treatise.
He was fascinated by the modern day reaction to Otzi the Iceman, found immaculately preserved on the Austrian side of the Alps in 1991 after 5,000 years.
First came bizarre stories that his penis had disappeared -- either eaten by a wild animal, snapped off by macabre collectors or cut off by a cuckolded husband who had caught him out.
But his penis and testicles were eventually found. They had just shrunk after years of cold and icy dryness.
Rumours that they still contained viable sperm prompted some Austrian women to volunteer for artificial insemination.
"Otzi may well have had children in his own lifetime and there is a fair chance that some of his direct descendants are alive in Alpine Europe today, 200 or so generations later."
"Thus some of the women wanting insemination with Otzi's sperm might be his great-great-great...granddaughters," Taylor wrote.
OPPRESSION OF WOMEN BEGAN WITH FARMING

Cave man may have grunted, clubbed his mate and carried her off for sex but Taylor says problems really began for women with the invention of farming. He argues that this quickly led to their general oppression.

"The domestication of animals and the availability of animal milk in addition to breast milk meant that women could raise their children in quicker succession than before, becoming even more tied to hearth and home in the process," he writes.
Some biologists argue that humans are slaves to their genes but Taylor says most prehistoric communities were in control of their destiny and fully able to separate sex from reproduction.
He concludes that variety is indeed the spice of life -- especially if it keeps burgeoning birth rates under control.

"To maintain a sexual morality that is based on reproduction is nonsense and, at present world population levels, dangerous nonsense. The development and transmission of cultural knowledge offers our brightest hope for the future."
